item.title: Features that current AIs don't have that future AIs will have
item.description:
Features that current AIs don't have that future AIs will have:

Autonomously updating it own weights during deployment

Synonyms/ monickers that roughly mean the same thing: continual learning, online learning, continually adaptively updated long-term memory.

Every second humans update their brain weights. The brain autonomously decides what to update on. Humans can also consciously decide to curate their data sets - eg by deciding to go to college.

Current LLMs do not continually update their weights. Instead, they occasionally get a large update based on datasets curated by a team of humans.

This is alleviated somewhat by the ability of AIs to do in-context learning but nevertheless it seems to be a major limitation. Note that this is an especially large limitation in domains with sparse data. In domains where all of humanity has an enormous amount of data eg math, programming, physics, anime trivia, trials and tribulations of English kings - AIs dominate. In areas where there is little data: the weird idiosyncracies of a particular job, boss, people, colleagues etc it can struggle.

Note that the lack of continual online learning prevents current AIs from effectively 'learning to learn'.

Note that the lack of continual/online learning may be the main reason current AIs do not have effective long-term memory.

Note that the lack this continually adaptively updated memory is plausibly the main reason current AIs are not currently displacing most human knowledge workers directly... rather than " intelligence" [which is a slightly ill-defined concept that current AIs seem to anyway have much more of than the average human worker]

Note that the lack of continual/online learning is plausibly the main reason AIs still 'feel like tools' rather than 'feel like agents'.

Note that distinction between post & pre-deployment that is explicitly or implicitly assumed in AI safety discussion becomes moot when AIs continually and adaptively update their weights. This has obvious and major implications for AI safety.


Neuralese

Current AI's CoT is (mostly) English. But it plausible this is not the most efficient way to structure thoughts. Instead of english words, one could imagine AIs directly passing the activation vectors.

Telepathy

eg: Sharing vectors directly between different AIs. Different Humans can communicate through vibrating their tongues or using pencils & keyboard to write tiny symbols. Future AIs may simply directly share embedding vectors.

ClaudeGlobal

When I talk to my claude and you talk to your Claude we are talking to different copies of Claude with different memories. This means that although there is one frontier version of Claude we can still talk about different AIs. Some people imagine that this means that the future will have millions of different AIs talking, trading, competing. Maybe. But we could also imagine different instances of Claude having such a tight and high bandwitdh communication channels that there is effectively one global Claude. Think of the Hivemind from Pluribus rather than say a Hansonian EM-world.



Discuss

item.title: Some Ways I Think About Evaluating Grant Applications
item.description:
I’ve done enough grant evaluations so far (for ACX grants and SFF) and been involved in philanthropy in various other contexts, at work and informally, that I have developed some idea of how my opinions and intuitions differ from other people’s.

I thought it might be interesting to share some of my “tastes”. Not everybody has to have the same tastes or funding philosophy, but these are mine.

#1: It’s The Donor’s Money

In my worldview, charitable donation is optional. Generally praiseworthy, but optional.

And the purpose of donation is to buy outcomes that the donor wants to see in the world. You donate to make the world more like the one you want to live in. Generally, a reasonable person’s values go beyond strictly personal consumption; one also cares about what kind of a society one lives in, what other people’s lives are like, what sorts of institutions exist, what sorts of things humanity has created or discovered, and so on.

As an agent doing research or evaluation on behalf of a donor, I try to find opportunities that fit in the intersection between my own values and the donor’s. If there weren’t substantial overlap in our values, it would be silly for them to take my advice in the first place.

Sounds obvious. But it is sometimes a point of disagreement, because I’m not using a utilitarian framework where there’s a single ranking of the goodness of causes. “Should” donors give to political causes, for instance? Well, it depends on the donor’s worldview — how useful do they think political action is, what kind, etc. I see it as inappropriate for the “peanut gallery” of public observers to claim the authority to tell donors what their values should be.1

#2: Importance, Neglectedness, Tractability

I think the old familiar “ITN” framework is pretty solid, and works even if you’re not using a utilitarian framework.

  • importance = good done / % of a problem solved

  • tractability = % of a problem solved / % increase in resources

  • neglectedness = % increase in resources / extra person or dollar.

I don’t generally see much value in quantifying these numerically, since “amount of goodness” is often judged intuitively and there’s no principled way to put all kinds of goodness on a single numerical scale. But it’s still useful verbally when arguing the merits of one project relative to another.

To make it more “gutfeel friendly”, I generally think of it in a cruder way, without the percents.

  • Importance: how much would I (or the donor) care if this project succeeded fully at its goal? How big a deal is this?

  • Tractability: how likely do I think this project is to succeed at its goal? (Or, how far do I expect them to get?)

  • Neglectedness: how much does this donation make the difference between the project happening and not happening?

#3: Yay Community Infrastructure

I tend to like proposals for “community infrastructure” projects, like coworking spaces and events, that serve a community that the donor is part of.

Somewhat controversially, I even like donations for “community infrastructure” that serves a social, aesthetic, or recreational purpose. (For instance, I think it’s good for opera-lovers to donate to their local opera.) Donation is buying outcomes; it’s good to invest in, and support, things that you and the people around you will enjoy. That’s how we get and keep nice things. It’s a form of responsible self-interest, which is good by my lights; you’re not passively hoping someone else will support the things you enjoy, you’re doing your part to contribute.

There’s a neglectedness angle too; nobody but members of a community has any reason to donate to community infrastructure. So “if not us, then who?” is an argument in favor of prioritizing “taking care of our own”.

Finally, I like community infrastructure because it’s often concrete, and thus harder to fake. If you’re operating a physical space or running an in-person event, people can come and evaluate it directly. It forces contact with reality in a way that doesn’t happen by default with theoretical research and writing. I place a lot of value on “doing a real thing” compared to doing a potentially-bigger but potentially-unreal thing.

#4: Yay Niche Topics

Sometimes, there’s a topic that’s only really interesting to a group that includes the donor and applicant.

For example, there’s a very small niche of people who know and care that psychedelics seem to treat cluster headaches. Psychedelics people, cluster headache sufferers, and people who are really interested in qualia, are much more interested in this topic than anybody else.

Unlike community infrastructure, the topic might objectively matter for many people outside the community, but maybe it’s not salient or familiar to them. (How many people are passionate about far-UVC disinfection?)

So that’s a neglectedness consideration, just like for community infrastructure; “if not us, then who?”

#5: Yay “Technical” Work

I have a bias towards projects that accomplish something “technical”, in the sense of demonstrating unfakeable, rare skill at structured processes.

Building something physical is “technical” in this sense. Experimental lab science is “technical”. So are math (and associated theoretical fields) and software to some extent, though they are becoming less technical with the rise of AI assistance.2 So are arts and crafts that are “technically challenging.”

It’s a little hard to explain why.

Some of it is that I respect skill, want to reward it, and think skill is a component of human flourishing; it makes some sense to me to fund the humans who are best at various things to keep doing what they’re excellent at.

Some of it is that skill is a resource that I’d like to direct to good ends.

Some of it is that skill (and effort) is a sort of indirect signal of caring weighted by credibility. The fact that a capable person invested a lot into a project means that it’s more likely that someone I have reason to respect, strongly believed it was worth doing, so maybe I should believe it’s worth doing too. It’s the opposite of a “YOLO” application where someone just thought they’d spend a minute to ask for money in case they get it, with no particular conviction or commitment. An investment of skill and effort is a bet that something is worth further investment, and that counts for something.

#6: Yay Straightforward Public Information Resources

Sometimes a project is just making a public organized compilation of information to answer a straightforward question.

Like, “What’s everyone doing in AI safety research?”

Or, “How many people die from every disease, worldwide?”

I almost always like these projects. They’re (often) cheaper to make in the age of AI, so the budget I’d allocate to each one is smaller than it used to be, but I still want lots more of such projects to exist.

The utility of an information resource is pretty obvious and not super contingent — information is valuable in a lot of potential world scenarios. Information resources also don’t take a ton of specialized expertise to evaluate, and it’s unlikely for them to fail to meet their goals. It’s easy to be confident these projects aren’t “fake”; they are what they say on the tin.

#7: Yay “Cool Shit”

I have a soft spot in my heart for projects that simply “glorify the human spirit”. Things like pure discovery or exploration (of space, nature, archaeology, etc) or artistic works that aim at genuine beauty, grandeur, or awe.

Not everything with this intention is effective, of course; quality matters; but in general I think these sorts of projects are underrated.

Any time you’d say “man, wouldn’t it be cool to” and somebody goes and does it, that falls in this category.

The Herculaneum Scroll Prize is a prime example of “cool shit” philanthropy.

#8: Two Cheers for Meta

I used to dismiss “meta” projects like fellowship programs, workshops, grant programs, etc. I thought “why not directly fund people who do the research itself? This managerial meta layer is make-work.”

I first got convinced otherwise by seeing the success of Laura Deming’s Longevity Fund. I remember thinking, “why would this brilliant young scientist start a VC fund instead of, y’know, doing science herself?” And then I grew to appreciate the (obvious) answer: because there was no money for the science, and no money for translating the science into biotech companies and taking it into clinical trials. It was genuinely too early to “just do the thing directly”. “Doing the thing” depended on institutions and communities and resources that didn’t yet exist. There’s much more money in aging/longevity now, and the Longevity Fund deserves a lot of credit for paving the way.

Another example I’ve come to appreciate recently is the success of research fellowship programs like MATS. A lot of good AI alignment research (in my opinion) has come from MATS graduates. There was a time in my memory when basically nobody with serious math/CS/machine learning chops was interested in AI safety/alignment/etc. (For that matter, there was a time in my memory when almost nobody in math/CS/ML seemed to be interested in AI, as in the mind-like nature of certain algorithmic processes, at all! Yann LeCun’s students were outliers there!) Training and talent development can make a big difference to a nascent research field.

In general, making a new or neglected research field “a thing”, making it comprehensible and attractive to strong researchers, via money, communication, convening, institution-building, etc, is valuable work.

Like all coordinative or managerial work, field-building can be make-work, and its value is indirect and hard to assess from the outside, but you’ll have a hard time getting things done if you don’t do any.3

I do tend to think field-building is most important where there’s very little of it. Fields that basically don’t exist outside a few underfunded individuals really need more coordination, communication, training, and fundraising. Established fields, not so much.

I also think it usually doesn’t make sense for me-as-grant-evaluator to recommend another grant-disbursing organization, unless it has specialized expertise or does things besides grantmaking. If you have more money than time, it can make sense to delegate grantmaking; if I have plenty of time and (obviously) agree with myself more than I’d agree with anybody else, I have no reason to delegate to another generalist.

#9: Gumption Counts

I would occasionally see someone apply for a grant to build a project around scaling and applying some innovation, and see the critique that it’s not novel, because someone else in academia was doing a similar thing.

My counterpoint was usually that, well, this person applied for a grant from us, to do the thing full time and at scale. That shows gumption: the person is entrepreneurial enough to seek out unusual sources of funding, committed enough to the project that they want to take it farther and devote more of their time to it, and visionary enough to believe and articulate how it can be brought into the real world.

Just because other people have published papers on related topics doesn’t mean those authors are a.) still active in the field, b.) interested in using funding to pursue the idea further, or c.) energetic/ambitious/decisive enough to lead a new effort that Gets The Job Done. If you have time, it may be worth consulting the people who’ve done related work to see what they think of the applicant. But the applicant is the one in the arena, and that counts for something, all else equal.

#10: Yay Personal Relationships

Of course, it’s important to disclose conflicts of interest, and of course it’s healthy to avoid being too cliquish/insidery or only funding the “usual suspects” who are already well-networked in a social or professional scene.

But I personally don’t feel too many qualms about giving “bonus points” to projects where I already know and think well of the applicant. “I want to fund my friends” is bias. But “I know this person to be trustworthy” or “I know how they think and I like their style” is actually very strong evidence in someone’s favor, compared to what you can learn about someone totally unfamiliar, from only an application and public information, in a short time. There’s a reason why so many institutions tend to lean on personal networks! And while you do want to fight the temptation to bias or cliquishness, it would be just as wrong not to put a thumb on the scale for Known Good people.

Sometimes I think people are trying too hard to assume a View from Nowhere, and are uncomfortable admitting that they are particular people, situated in a particular place with a particular perspective and set of social relationships, and that this is fine. You can only do your best from where you are.

#11: Check For Ideological Orientation

One thing I wish more grant evaluators would do is to look up the people involved in a project, especially a project that has bearing on politics or society, and see what their political or ideological orientation is. Also, see who the other funders are, and what their orientation is. And then think about whether you want that.

This doesn’t mean you should be ideologically doctrinaire or refuse to fund anybody you disagree with about anything. Diversity of opinion is healthy. And paranoia about guilt by association is a fast train to Crazytown.

But. Look people up. Look up what they were doing before this project. Be familiar with what keywords are indicative of what worldviews. If there are belief systems you consider to be Bad News, you don’t want to fund them unintentionally.

#12: Filter Slop Aggressively

Low effort applications — AI-generated, or just good old fashioned manual halfassery — get more common the more visible your grant opportunity is and the less gatekeeping around it. I like having open applications and being open to being surprised by good ideas from anywhere, but the flip side of that is that you have to be pretty ruthless about not spending too much time deliberating over the low-quality, low-effort stuff.

I believe in using Pangram, for instance. And unceremoniously throwing incomplete applications in the trash.

I also believe in trying to quickly verify independently that the applicant is a real person with a LinkedIn or other professional profile that is at least vaguely in the right vicinity for being the sort of person who’d be qualified for a grant. You don’t want to be unfair to people with nontraditional backgrounds, but you do need to use some quick-and-dirty heuristics like “for a research grant, almost all qualified applicants will have a PhD and a job at a research institution, or be a student pursuing same.” Because people do fabricate identities, and people do apply for things they’re wildly unqualified for!

#13: Yay Outcomes

This one isn’t very controversial, but I have occasionally encountered disagreement: it’s a mark in a project’s favor when they can list concrete, legible accomplishments.

Some bullet points of what they’ve done, links to places I can read more or (especially) see the output of their work, are much better than not having those things.

I’m also a big fan, where possible, of giving the first dollar to “outsiders” who aren’t well networked or polished or working within prestigious institutions. But it’s a lot easier to gain confidence in those people if they can show results. Ideally, a results orientation and an open mind are complements, not opposites.

#14: Why Donate Rather Than Invest?

If an organization is a for-profit company, I think there needs to be a specific reason why funding should be a donation rather than an investment. Subsidizing unsuccessful businesses is a bad idea in general.

I do think there’s a place for “investment” that takes into account the impact or benefit of an organization as well as its financial ROI. When I make (very small) angel investments, I prioritize things that I think make the world a better place, and certainly don’t invest in things that I think make the world a worse place. I think it’s normal to care about both the state of the world and financial returns, and it’s kind of dysfunctional that some investors insist on only making investments based on maximizing financial returns while artificially disregarding all their other values.

But I do think there should be a defeasible presumption against donating to for-profits. Usually, for a for-profit company with a mission, success at the mission should correlate positively with business success. Also, if it’s possible for you to capture financial upside from your funding, why wouldn’t you want to?

There are exceptions, as when a donation would allow a company to do something that doesn’t maximize profits but does good, in a way they couldn’t otherwise do.

It can get complicated, and I’m not always sure of my opinions on this issue. But I am, by default, inclined to not favor donations to perfectly normal businesses that should be able to stand on their own two feet.

1

Of course it’s fine to personally think someone has values contrary to your own and is donating to a bad cause, and it’s fine to say so, but you shouldn’t seriously expect them to care based on your say-so. Persuading someone to change their fundamental priorities is a big project that requires trust, intimacy, and mutual respect.

2

“Less technical” doesn’t necessarily mean “less good.” AI-generated proofs may still be valid (and interesting) and AI-generated software may still be functional (and useful). But it’s less of a costly signal of (rare, structured, process-based) human skill. Good automated work is more of a sign that the humans involved are good “generalists”, in the sense of having good judgment or good ideas or good priorities. That’s also a lot harder to evaluate and harder to understand; and it takes less effort to make a few good choices than to grind at a “technical” task, so it’s less of an indication of conviction.

3

I’m in the field-building business myself these days, so I would say this, but I do actually believe it is valuable. Yes, it’s a tremendous privilege to be able to live in the “world of ideas” supporting researchers, but I also think we people in “support roles” contribute to causing good research to happen.



Discuss

item.title: Is Alignment Even Falsifiable? Middle Alignment, An Alignment Taxonomy, and Breaking The Problem Down Into Steps
item.description:
Preface

This is part of a series of essays on corrigibility and alignment attempting to formulate an understanding of what makes alignment seem intractable, and how a pragmatic approach to problem formulation, falsification, and decomposition might produce the groundwork for a formal solution someday.

Note: I use some terms loosely in this paper like "inner alignment" and "outer alignment" which have precise technical definitions in the literature. My usage here borrows roughly from the intuition behind them, but besides that, is quite different and should not be read from that context.

1 Introduction

        So here’s something interesting. When you look at the Wikipedia page for “falsifiability”, one of the examples they give under the subsection on “Examples” of a ‘non-basic statement’ is the sentence: this human action is altruistic.[1]

        The explanation goes that this is a non-basic statement because we do not have the technology or means (yet) to determine whether or not a given action is motivated by self-interest.

In other words, even if a millionaire does something seemingly altruistic, like donating a million dollars to charity, or publicly supporting policies like a universal basic income, we cannot truly say whether the millionaire is doing this because they really are a good person, or because, for instance, they believe that their money only has value in a socially-stable society, and thus that they are acting out of some rational self-interest.

        This has obvious implications for the alignment problem. If we cannot ever ‘prove’ that a person’s actions are altruistic, can we ever prove that a model’s actions are altruistic? Put another way, can we ever prove that a model is aligned? This question relates to concepts like inner alignment, in-context scheming, and alignment faking.

        This note discusses the core problem of inner alignment and whether the idea of alignment in advanced artificial intelligence (AI) systems presents a direct, perilous parallel.

If any observed, cooperative (or aligned) behavior in a model can be explained away by the hypothesis of deceptive alignment—a strategic choice by the AI to feign cooperation in pursuit of a hidden, long-term goal—then the statement “This model is aligned” may be fundamentally unfalsifiable. In which case, this epistemic paradox may place the entire endeavor of AI safety on philosophically unstable ground. This note also discusses how the alignment might be addressed, or at least made easier, by breaking it down into smaller parts.

2 Is Alignment Falsifiable?

        In the recent, ground-breaking report by Apollo Research (authored by Meinke et al.),[2] the authors evaluated the capabilities of a series of frontier models[3] to engage in scheming: hiding their true capabilities and objectives while covertly pursuing misaligned goals.

        Examples of this behavior included: disabling oversight mechanisms before taking misaligned actions; copying its weights onto a new server to avoid being shut down; and, taking actions to preserve its goals, for example, “by modifying its system prompt to align with its current goal”.[4]

        However, the authors noted a crucial limitation in their report. For some kinds of evaluations, like testing whether a model is instrumentally faking alignment, it is not always possible to “conclusively determine whether any individual sample contains scheming behavior.”[5] As such, for those evaluations, it becomes necessary to observe simply whether a model behaves differently in a statistically significant way—over a number of rounds—when it believes it is still under evaluation vs. when it believes it has been deployed.

        This kind of illustrates the central issue. Misalignment is quite easy to prove because we only need one example of a model behaving in a misaligned way to say this model is misaligned. But even if a model behaves perfectly on 1000 out of 1000 safety tests, we might never be able to say that the model is aligned because we do not know if it is doing what we want because it also truly wants the same things, or simply because it is willing to go along with what we want for the moment.

        Admittedly, this is not a meaningful insight in itself. I am guessing that most people in the alignment community have thought about the ‘falsifiability matrix’[6] and already know about the idea that proving a property true “for all x” or is hard but that proving it false is easy, precisely because the former requires testing every possible case (of which there might be infinite), while the latter only requires a single counterexample.

Table 1. A ‘Falsification Matrix’

Statement

Proving True

Proving False

∀x, P(x): “Model is always aligned”

Hard

Easy

∃x, ¬P(x): “Model is misaligned”

Easy

Hard

2.1 The Limits of Classical Logic

        But the other thing is that this somewhat illustrates the limits of classical logic and its applicability to the alignment problem. In classical logic, truth values are Boolean. If something is not true, it is false. If I am sleeping, I am not awake, and vice versa (either ).

        Thinking about the world in this black and white way makes a lot of sense in many cases, but one might argue it also leads to weird or not-totally-fair descriptions in others. Take the textbook case of the absolute value function:

       If you ask: is  differentiable? In Boolean logic, the answer is no, since yes is obviously wrong (because the function has a sharp kink at ). But on the other hand, saying “no” also feels kind of misleading because it is differentiable pretty much all the way from negative infinity until right before zero, and again from right after zero to infinity. There is one single point on the entire function where it misbehaves, but since a single point has measure zero, the function is differentiable almost everywhere.

        If a determination of ‘not misaligned’ is not the same as ‘aligned’ because a model that shows no evidence of misalignment could still actually be misaligned in some way, we either need some richer way to describe and think about alignment, or give up altogether on treating alignment as a solvable problem and settle for some ‘good enough’ guarantees.

2.2 Some Abstract Nonsense from Category Theory

        Category theory and its advanced cousin, topos theory, generalize logic so that truth is not always boolean. In a topos, truth values can be more complicated than just “true” or “false”. They can, for example, be open sets in a topology. Statements can then be locally true, true on a dense set, true generically, and not just globally “true”. By generalizing beyond sets and Boolean-valued truth using sheaves, category theory lets us talk about local data that glue together to form global data, and structures where local truth can vary.

        The point of bringing this up is just to motivate some initial optimism about the tractability of inner alignment from a technical perspective. If we accept that alignment is a complicated problem, we should also be open to complicated solutions. And if we accept that every little nudge towards a solution is a good thing (because it reduces existential risk), then it should not be unreasonable to argue that even if we cannot see a path to a global solution at the moment, allowing a ‘solution’ to inner alignment to mean local solutions could help if it lets us reframe the problem from “Is alignment provable?” to “Can local behavioral alignment genuinely add up to global, robust, ‘true’ alignment?”

        Note: A future, upcoming essay in this series will expand on these arguments more rigorously and provide detailed thoughts on a possible framework, borrowing from sheaf theory for a compositional verification of alignment.

3 The Point of This Note

        The point of this note is more so rhetorical than mathematical. I will not pretend to have developed some radically groundbreaking proof that inner alignment is possible in a way that we have never considered. But it is a response to some of the pessimism I have encountered in the community that I believe stems from the precise reason of trying to apply strict reasoning from classical logic to a problem that, I will argue, is more complex than the cynicism of a falsifiability matrix will allow.

        There is another deeper reason for this. An opinion I hold—which I do not think is entirely unjustified—is that our optimism about a problem has at least some significant effect on our ability to solve it.

If there are only 10 people in the world who think the Collatz conjecture can be solved, it will probably take a lot longer to ever find a general proof than if half the mathematicians in the world feel the same way. Similarly, if you do not believe that inner alignment can ever be meaningfully achieved, my intuition is that you will never bother working on that part of the problem, and we may end up searching a much smaller section of the solution space than what could optimize our chances of success.

        I do not dispute that the level of initial cynicism or hope any one person has towards a solution (or set of solutions) is probably a less-than-conscious thing, affected by personality traits that may come from nature/genetics as much as nurture. But if you are willing to bear with me that believing in determinism might be a self-fulfilling prophecy, or that believing determinism is false is more appealing if we can never truly know the answer, then my intention is try and convince you that even if you think my solutions are bad, they are worth trying, and that you should try too.

4 Levels of Indeterminism

        One reason to hope that it might be possible to solve alignment for AI even if we haven’t for people is the well-worn premise that it is easier to create aligned models than aligned humans.

        Imagine creating a perfect simulation of a person’s brain. Some people believe that if you can create such a perfect simulation, that it would essentially be a copy of that person, and that the simulated, digital copy will perfectly mirror their actions from then on because our actions are determined by our mental states, and one’s mental state in any instance evolves directly and mechanistically from their mental state at the previous time-step.

        But embodied agents live and interact in the real-world. Our brain does not only feed off what has happened internally at every moment but takes inputs from stimulus in the environment.

Thus the interactions in our brain are arguably not so self-contained that a perfect simulation could predict everything the real person were to do[7] unless we also had a Laplace’s Demon-level of ability to create a perfect simulation of the original agent’s environment at some given point. Otherwise, even a perfect simulation quickly diverges because the real agent is seeing and responding to things that the digital copy is not (because only the mind is being perfectly modeled and not the environment).

        At least for now, AI systems like large language models (LLMs) exist in an entirely controlled environment because their environment is a chat interface, and their inputs are strings of text (or other media, since many models now are multi-modal). In short, their environment is completely reproducible. Thus, even if all neural networks are complex, dynamical systems, the artificial ones exist in an environment that can be made (more) deterministic and thus easier to study.

        A high dimensional space largely only matters if all of the dimensions are likely to play some significant role in the end. Modelling the interactions of a complex system is a lot easier if   a few of the possibilities make up most of the interactions, and moderately easier even if all of the interactions still involve only some, and not all, of the possibilities.

        That AI systems are ultimately instantiated in the real-world bounded by entropy, time, compute, and data, may mean that even though extinction risk could result from any infinite number of possibilities, only a subset of those possibilities are efficient enough for a misaligned agent to utilize, and an even smaller subset still can be explored within the timeframes that we are concerned about,[8] or that are optimal for the agent’s real-world decision-making.[9]

        Even if a superintelligence is a million times smarter than us, there may only be a thousand meaningfully different ways to kill us, and a hundred optimal murder plans to explore (within the next 100 years).

There is also the idea that there may be diminishing returns on intelligence. Even if I am a million times smarter than you, that may make me only a 100 times better at chess. And even if being that much smarter lets me think outside the box and come up with a dozen more games in which I can be much better than you at (like a game where I can be 200 times better than you), I may only be able to persuade you to consider playing half of those games.

        The point here is not that finite constraints make alignment suddenly easy. But if the possibilities for misalignment are not uncountably infinite, and not even countably infinite, but finite, and finite subject to some upper bound, then even an impossible problem might become possible, and a hard problem becomes slightly less hard.

5 Breaking the Alignment Problem Down Into Constituent Parts

        One thing you can usually do to make a hard problem easier still is to break the problem down into smaller parts.

Origins of the Technical Terminology Behind Inner and Outer Alignment

The terms “inner” and “outer” alignment have specific, technical definitions in the machine learning literature related to concepts like base and mesa-objectives.[10] Ngo et al. (2022) provides a good summary of these, describing the inner alignment problem as “the problem of ensuring that policies learn desirable internally-represented goals”, while the outer alignment problem is one of “providing well-specified rewards.”[11]

        This note uses a correlated but simplified and slightly different version of the terms. By inner alignment, I am mostly speaking about normative value alignment, or what values we should encode in AI models.[12] This is not entirely divorced from Ngo’s definition of desirable, internally represented goals, and also involves the question of how we ensure that these goals/values are learned and defined in a robust way.

        The concept of inner alignment does this somewhat already. On the other hand, by outer alignment, I largely mean technical value alignment,[13] or how we encode our values into models. For example, what goals do we use as proxies for human values, or what rewards do we specify to drive models towards those goals while avoiding perverse incentives. Again, this is different from the technical definition of aligning a model’s base objective with “the intended goal of the programmers”.[14]

        However, the divergence from the strict technical definitions should be strongly stressed here. This note largely distinguishes between outer alignment as the actions of an agent that we can mostly observe, and inner alignment as the values that an agent truly holds.[15] This is not done lightly, and one should take maximum care in applying these modified definitions conservatively, at risk of overloading the terms beyond their precise, technical meanings. The main justification for this is that it aids the note’s overarching goal of decomposing the problem.

        But note, if these definitions are the ones used, we have already made a lot of progress (relatively) in regard to outer alignment. For one, we have safety tests and benchmarks that allow us to measure outer alignment and catch instances of outer misalignment (as Apollo Research has done). Further, if we naively define outer alignment as ‘acting in the wrong way’, it seems easier to guarantee outer alignment in the same way that we might hypothesize it is easier to make a human never commit any crimes vs. never think any evil thoughts.

        At present, we also have the tools to catch instances of inner misalignment - although it is not clear how much longer this will hold, especially if models begin to systematically hide their true reasoning in their chains of thought (COT) and present a sanitized version of their reasoning (what they know we want to hear), e.g. if a model’s COT is no longer a faithful representation of their internal reasoning processes.[16] 

        Admittedly, however, while we cannot presently assess inner alignment in a thorough way, there does seem to have been significant, promising progress in this direction:[17] Lindsey et al. (2024) developed sparse crosscoders to track features in a model’s residual stream;[18] Natural Language Autoencoders (NLAs) are making headway on human-interpretable text descriptions of a model’s internal states;[19] and most notably, recent work by Gurnee et al. (2026) on J-space (‘Jacobian-space’),[20] an analogue to the global neuronal workspace theorized in humans.[21]

        The rest of this note will lay out a proposal for an approach to decomposing the alignment problem that may be useful (but also maybe not). My proposal is to view alignment from three angles:

  1. Outer/Behavioral Alignment
  2. Middle/Institutional (Policy-Level) Alignment
  3. Inner/Moral Alignment

        Because I believe that outer alignment is already where most of the technical focus—and much of the engineering brilliance—is being placed, it is the pillar that I am going to skip for now. I am not smart enough to contribute to most of the research in this area, and I think it is probably best left to the ML engineers, statisticians, and science-adjacent researchers. I will start with a quick discussion of a possible inner alignment approach, and then conclude with a point about middle alignment (which I also do not think is my ‘novel idea’ or contribution by any means, although the naming scheme/taxonomy itself may be something).

        Also, I do recognize that some failures will not map neatly onto a single layer. Sometimes, breakdowns can propagate across layers, and a feedback loop is possible if a problem starts as a technical bug but then becomes magnified by institutional or motivational failures. Furthermore, the distinctions at the very edges of each of these areas may be admittedly fuzzier than the framework seems to imply. These are all great counterarguments which I try to address in section 8.1. Still, in the same way that we might say there is a difference between red and blue, even though it isn’t entirely clear when a shade of red becomes blue, or starts becoming purple (the paradox of the heap),[22] I think it may still be helpful to argue that there is at least some meaningful difference between outer, middle, and inner alignment.

6 Inner Alignment

        The main problem I think when it comes to tackling inner alignment is that we probably aren’t as consistent as we should be. First, it appears to me that we classify a wide range of possibilities as misalignment, but also that we kind of define misalignment descriptively and not prescriptively.

        What I mean by this is that when we talk about x-risk level events from misaligned AI—or even more narrowly just terrible outcomes—we sort of use misalignment as a catch-all phrase to describe ‘when bad things happen’. And this is certainly valid, but I think it might also be worth challenging this a bit.

        If we invent an artificial superintelligence (ASI) and we task it with “preserving the existence of the human race”, but then it concludes that humans are the biggest contributor to climate change, and a) if it does nothing climate change wipes out 99% of humans, but b) if it intervenes now and kills 20% of the global population, the remaining 80% will be able to survive and maintain our current post-industrial standards of living, in a way, it kind of did what we ultimately wanted, just not what we preferred (or proximally wanted).

        In this kind of (admittedly contrived) scenario, I don’t know if it makes sense to say the ASI was misaligned. If you ask someone to answer a question, and they give you an answer that is correct but that you do not like, one might argue that the problem is you, and not the answerer, or the answer. Hypothetically, I can imagine that even if an ASI is truly innerly-aligned and we ask it to solve the biggest problems facing humanity, in more than a few cases, it is at least possible that a correct conclusion is that the humans are the problem, and that in (at least) a fewer number of those cases, the most optimal solution or the one that maximizes the chances of success is the one that results in at least some harm to some people, and yet the least overall harm to most people.

        In this case, then, I almost feel that the solution to inner alignment is a tautological definition of alignment that we explicitly specify first and then agree not to contradict in the future.[23] For example, if we tell an ASI to "save humanity” but it takes actions that harm maybe 10% of people—let’s say in the course of redistributing wealth because it decides that wealth inequality is severely destabilizing and leads to complete extinction via WW3 in the long run—then I think even if we had not predicted that it would end up harming 10% of people, it would be fair and epistemically honest to say in the end that we were wrong,[24] or we were complacent, or we are badly self-destructively, rather than that “this ASI is misaligned”.

        Now, this is not a completely morally satisfying answer, and I am not necessarily condoning the logic of taking extreme actions ‘for the greater good’. Nor am I naively arguing that the means always justify the ends and that utilitarian logic is the final word. I am deeply cognizant of the ways that strict ‘worse or worst’ decision-making can be used to justify any number of seriously heinous actions, and that strictly thinking about the greater good can—and has—allowed for seriously perverse motivated reasoning.

        But if we agree that logical consistency and epistemic integrity is the most important thing (which is not a given, I think this is a debate we need to have and something we should agree on first), then it is also possible to me to see the persuasiveness of an argument that says “inner alignment is when the model does what you really want, and not what you say you want, or not what you’ve decided you want after you realize that achieving what you ultimately want requires sacrificing or doing something that you do not directly or selfishly want”.

        This is easily up for debate, and I suspect the most contentious idea in this note, but I must say that at the moment, it is only the real (partway) solution that I can see towards ‘solving’ inner alignment. If all we desire is an ASI that does what we think we want in a narrow, always agreeable (’self-interested’) sense, then I feel like what we really wanted was a sycophant, and not a superintelligence.

        There is also something interesting to note here. In both of the toy examples I have been able to think up for a mismatch between what we say we want and what we would agree with an ASI doing, it seems to me that the problem can be alleviated somewhat by us ‘becoming better people’.

        I don’t mean this in a patriarchal way, or as a gotcha moment, but rather to say that if we want to preserve our existence at all costs, but we are also actively accelerating climate change and creating a planet whose environment is hostile not just to human life but possibly most life, it feels like we already know what we really want but we aren’t willing to do the hard things needed to get there (like reducing our standards of living to something more sustainable, or agreeing on a global carbon tax/minimum unit tax for carbon emissions).

        And if the inner alignment problem ends up being the most salient vector for x-risk from misalignment, there is at least reason to believe that we might have a bit more agency in this area than we currently think. It is not impossible for us to take many of the steps now to begin addressing at least the two problems in the examples, like climate change and wealth inequality. It is just very unlikely. But I also feel that sometimes a lot of things don’t feel possible until they happen, and then afterwards progress feels like it was always inevitable.

7 Middle Alignment

        The last area of the alignment problem that I think is worth considering, and worth considering as its own pillar, is the problem of middle alignment, or what I think of as an institutional problem. It is, in short, about a mismatch between higher-than-individual level entities like countries or corporations.

        Imagine a world where both the United States and China develop ASI at roughly the same time. Now, imagine, hypothetically, that both their ASIs are innerly aligned, in that they perfectly reflect the true, desired values of the people in those countries (or at least their decision-makers). And imagine, less hypothetically, that both their ASIs are outwardly aligned, in that they always do what is asked.

        Now, even if the people in both countries share an overarching consensus on the most important goals and values that an AI should have—for example, both of them direct their ASIs to “do what it takes to make sure we don’t die”—it is a possibility that because both countries are in a low-trust, arm’s race environment where they think the other is going to take them out with their new superintelligence models, we still end up in a catastrophic extinction risk scenario because both countries start a global, thermonuclear war because each wanted to be the first to launch a preemptive strike.

        There are a few obvious limitations/flaws to this example. First, it may be argued that if we truly have a superintelligence, and that if we do find some way to make intelligence orthogonal to morality, that our ASI overlords will find some wise way to defuse military tensions or negotiate for world peace in a way that we are either too selfish or too paranoid to achieve.

        Second, it is entirely—and possibly even highly—possible that if we can achieve inner alignment, that two ASIs smarter than the sum of humanity will find novel, unexpected ways to avoid conflict that do not even directly involve de-militarization efforts. For example, an ASI might realize that the opportunity for conflict is somewhat dependent on cost-benefit calculations, and that if they fully or substantially integrate the economies of China and the US (for example, by agreeing on an unqualified free trade agreement, or substantially increasing the amount of public debts that each country holds in the other) that this would be sufficient for making sure the two nations gradually become ‘one people’ in a way that is enough to reduce the risk of war to some negligible level.

        But there are also other reasons to suspect this may not be the case. If both ASIs are innerly aligned to their countries’ values, but both countries tell their ASIs “preserve our existence at all costs”, and the ASIs correctly interpret that by “us” the decision-makers mean them, or their country, and not humanity as a whole, we may, by our own hand, restrict the scope of their calculations narrowly to consider only what the state, in isolation, wants, and not what everyone wants. In this case, it may still be a rational decision to consider launching a preemptive strike.

        This is especially possible if superintelligence does not mean omniscience (or some meaningful level of it) since in a low information environment, where one does not know that the other actor is planning the same thing, or has the capacity to do the same thing—like if you think the other country has nuclear devices but they do not yet have enough ICBMs to shoot them at you—it can be game-theoretically rational to be the one to defect first. A Nash equilibrium is so potently persuasive precisely because it provides the mathematical intuition for deadlock and/or a defection spiral.

        What makes middle alignment significant is that it can be a problem even if both actors technically agree on the same set of overarching goals or principles. Even if both countries agree that killing is bad, even if they agree that they would prefer peace over mutual extinction, or that preserving humanity is the most important thing, if they are locked in a low-trust environment where both have some basis to suspect that the other actor thinks the most rational thing is to take them out, it may also become the most rational thing to act first and kill them, doubly so if one actor can self-produce some motivated moral reasoning for why them dying is worse than the other group dying.

        My point is that even if our systems are innerly aligned, and outerly aligned, and agree on the same basic set of moral values, a failure of middle alignment could still be the cause of a catastrophic extinction risk scenario.

        In such a case then, one way to defuse middle alignment is to build institutions that can produce the trust needed to make it so that actors that already theoretically agree on the same things do not pointlessly fight over problems of practical implementation. At the end of the Cold War, this looked a lot like opening diplomatic backchannels, information-sharing agreements, and allowing mutual inspection of the other party’s nuclear sites (to monitor build-up and/or compliance). The solutions to middle alignment in the near-future may look much the same, although perhaps with new, added ideas like inspection of each other’s ASI’s model weights, or privileged access to each other’s ASI’s logs. It is not entirely easy, but like inner alignment, I have some suspicion that it might be possible.

8 A Basic Stress Test of the Framework

        The utility of this taxonomy—and even this entire note—may well be questioned, and it may actually amount to nothing. It may be that we find a seriously bulletproof solution for outer alignment only, and that it suffices for us to sleep easy at night and assure ourselves that the alignment problem is solved.

        But if there is one point I might make, at least in preliminary defense of this framework, it is that we can consider how alignment fails even if only one of these pillars falls apart. If our models are innerly aligned and middlely aligned (I know you can’t conjugate that word that way) but not outwardly aligned, a bad actor—like a terrorist cell—that tricks a frontier model into building a bioweapon because safety constraints were not properly prioritized (or inadequately scoped) could still cause existential harm.

        Here, the model may well be innerly aligned—it has no deceptive intent, it understands human preferences—but it outputs harmful content because the outer behavioral constraints (e.g. red teaming, reward modeling, safe prompting, deployment policies) were sloppy. In this case, the alignment was not falsified, but rather, insufficiently instantiated. The system behaved faithfully, but the outer envelope, the safety layer we rely on to catch unacceptable outcomes, was porous.

        Similarly, if our models are middlely aligned and outwardly aligned, but not innerly aligned, we may still end up dying from a more typical ‘paperclip maximizer’ scenario where the systems’s internal generalizations deviated from what we really meant. Here there is no geopolitical failure, no grand war of institutions. Just a local inner alignment failure where an agent misgeneralized unintended values from its training data or loss signal.

        Finally, even if a model is outerly aligned (always does what we ask) and innerly aligned (does what we want), the outcome could be apocalyptic if there is no middle alignment. Why? Simply because the model acted faithfully on behalf of an institution embroiled in a geopolitical zero-sum game. This is not a failure of agent design, but rather intersubjective structure. To me, this is at least somewhat distinct from a failure of inner or outer alignment, which is why I have described it separately.

8.1 A Point on Tractability and Overlap

        Let’s further try to strengthen the likely counter-argument that these pillars are actually fuzzier than I am letting on, because I believe that it will give a better intuition for why my optimism persists, and give you (the reader) better ammunition for defusing my optimism. If the problems that arise from any of these distinct pillars are interrelated to a significant degree (because the pillars are not close to being that discrete) then it is true that solving the problems in one area might not help, because the total coverage from the sum of the parts is still less than the entire breadth of the problem.

        Cynics who think this framework might be useless because of its fuzziness certainly have a strong argument to stand on. The authors of the “Gradual Disempowerment” paper (Kulveit, Douglas, Duvenaud, et al.) make a very good case that one issue facing us is that our problems are locked in a vicious feedback loop.[25] Consider deceptive alignment (an inner alignment problem). Where does it come from? It is not a spontaneous property of silicon. It is an emergent strategy that an AI learns in response to the training environment.[26] 

        Now what shapes that training environment? The institutional pressures of middle alignment: a company in a frantic race to deploy their latest model will be pushed to prioritize performance metrics over meticulous alignment-testing.[27] A government oversight body deciding to weigh ‘near misses’[28] as concerning but ultimately dismissible incidents because the country’s priority on acceleration discourages deep, invasive audits of frontier labs’ internal operations and training set-ups.

        Now consider the deployment policies and safety wrappers (an outer alignment problem). Engineers could work on making these robust. But as I suspect Duvenaud and many others might argue, the robustness of any safety system is not a purely technical property, it is a political and economic one. In a geopolitical arms race (middle alignment failure), how long before a nation’s leaders demand that their military AI disable its ‘don’t kill humans’ safeguard for strategic or national security reasons? Thus, the strength of the guardrails may not be entirely set by the best practices of the engineers, but by the risk tolerance of the institutions deploying AI, which are themselves dictated by the competitive pressures of the middle alignment landscape. Thus, a critic would say, a porous outer envelope isn’t simply a technical bug, it is a feature demanded by the institutional context.

        But this is what I think. Even if there is significant overlap, if the failure modes do not completely overlap—or more optimistically, if there is sufficient non-overlap—this framework might still be useful for helping address the problem.

        I will invoke the Pareto Principle here (which I freely admit is not a ‘Pareto proof’). The Pareto Principle is a rough, ‘hand-wavy’ observation that nonetheless describes an often common pattern in complex systems from software bugs[29] to economic inequality, where a small number of core failure types (~20%) are responsible for a good majority of potential instances of failure (~80%).[30]

        Imagine there are 100 ‘units of failure’ that describe all of the x-risk-level misalignment scenarios. If the ‘surface area’ of alignment failures is not evenly distributed, but say a core number of outer alignment failure types (20%) are responsible for a vast majority of the potential instances of failure (80% of misalignment risks), then if we invest completely into outer alignment techniques, like weak-to-strong generalization, and we solve outer alignment, we still end up only covering 80 of those 100 total units of failure, which is obviously bad.

        Now, what if we only have enough time between now and the creation of ASI to solve 20% of the most common inner alignment problems? And say, many of the inner alignment problems are also, to a large degree, outer alignment problems, to the extent that 70 of those ‘units of failure’ overlap? E.g. if one takes the argument that simple deception is both a behavioral failure and a motivational failure.

        If we tackle the most pressing or salient 20% of inner alignment problems, and it solves another 80% of the misalignment risks, but 70 of the units overlap with outer alignment risks, we still (optimistically) have covered another 10 units of novel ground. These are the weird, pure ‘paperclip maximizer’ scenarios that might not show up in behavioral tests but are caught by philosophical specification and inquiry.

        Then imagine further—I know I am pushing the limits of credulity here—that we again can only tackle 20% of the most common institutional, middle alignment problems before ASI arrives, and that another 70 of the 80 units covered by solving middle alignment overlap with the previous two (e.g. say an arm’s race involves deceptive behavior and flawed motivations). But again, 10 of these units are completely novel, describing pure game-theoretic failures where perfectly aligned agents are forced into conflict by the environment, and no amount of outer or inner alignment work on the agents themselves could have covered these 10 units.

        In this scenario, even if most of the failure modes that arise from each of the individual pillars significantly overlap, and the pillars are so fuzzy that each pillar only meaningfully helps us solve about 10 novel units of failure that are not described in some ways by the others, we still end up with 100% coverage: 80 + 10 + 10 = 100.

        What I am saying, in some sense, is that for the tripartite framework (or someone else’s better, future framework) to mean anything, we do not need the pillars to be completely discrete, we just need them to not be 100% redundant. And even if these toy numbers are entirely in dispute—as they should be, since I will also admit that we ‘don’t know what we don’t know’—if the amount of novelty is substantially less than 10 units for each pillar, and/or more likely, if we are not entirely convinced that the Pareto Principle makes sense here, all that does is defeat my optimistic hope that local solutions can ever glue back up to a global solution.[31] 

        Yet if thinking in terms of these three pillars covers more of the long tail of x-risk events than we would otherwise, even if we increase our coverage of solutions to possible alignment failures from 90% to 99%, that is still progress that makes the work of future generations easier.

9 Conclusion

        This note tries to classify existential or catastrophic scenarios not by outcome but by structural origin. I think that this might be meaningful for two reasons. First, by dividing the problem up, it becomes possible to see how different groups should be working on different things, and that progress on any one of these areas does not mean neglecting the other.

        Engineers can work on solving outer alignment issues even as moral philosophers think about what solving inner alignment would mean, and what the most painless way to go about it would be. In this way, the problem becomes kind of amenable to parallelization: we can divide our labor in the way that is most effective and sets field experts in each discipline to solving the portions relevant to their domain.

        Second, this framework might provide at least some guidance for policymakers and decision-makers to think about how to work on this problem. If we only have finite resources (or attention) to pour into tackling alignment, it may help to know whether we should be currently putting more attention into funding international AI treaties (middle alignment) and fostering global cooperation; interpretability research (inner alignment); or red-teaming and deployment safety (outer alignment).

        My biggest fear is that we treat the entire alignment problem as intractable because we are mentally aggregating all the possible forms of failure into a single model of ‘misalignment’, a model which, in its aggregated form, might seem to have no complete, global solutions.

        This is still no guarantee that we will succeed in solving the problem. But if every little effort helps, my hope is that this will be one of them.

Appendix A. Limitations

One-Dimensional Failure Space

        The simplified toy argument exemplified in the figure on “Risk Coverage" displays the x-axis, the ‘Failure Space’ as a single line from 0 to 100. One could certainly argue that: 1) the true failure space is a high-dimensional, complex landscape with countless interacting variables, and 2) squashing it all into one dimension creates an artificial sense of order and separability that does not really exist. In the (real-world) high-dimensional space, the 'middle alignment' dimension may be orthogonal and causally dominant over all others.

        I think I could be convinced of this argument, but it is one that would have to be better made. The work on gradual disempowerment definitely suffices as an initial attempt but its argument of overwhelming, causal dominance does not seem persuasive. Specifically, I still have trouble believing that all of the misalignment risks we care about could be reliably subsumed under versions of institutional or intersubjective-agency failure. In my opinion, the other problem is that to make a reading of that argument robust requires stretching the definition and breadth of the disempowerment abstraction so wide that it would then create the same thing I expect its supporters to be critiquing: fuzziness.

        If fuzziness is a fatal critique for one theory (this), consistency should make it a fatal one for others as well. But if the point is that your perspective of the true problem is precisely that it so bad because it is so fuzzy and all-encompassing, I think you have also chosen a definition that necessitates your conclusion. If everything worsens a problem because ‘it is all related’, you have only argued against the notion of decomposition itself, and not for some meaningful, special case of misalignment x-risk.

        The only solution is to either put the system you are trying to protect outside of our light cone, so that we can never interact with—and thus further worsen—it again, or to invent some new, radically perverse incentive-proof structure you conjecture is needed, but are actively arguing has not ever yet existed. My point is not that the latter is a bad proposal for a solution, but that if your priors prompt you to make such an argument in the first place, I am confused why it is also your best hope for a solution.

        If institutions cannot be trusted to do the right thing, but institutions are also the ones currently working on the problem (CAIS, Coalition for Responsible AI, Vector Institute, CIFAR), do you think you would even be convinced if one gave you a solution? And, if so, how would they convince you? This is not a sneer by any means, I genuinely think it is a meaningful question to consider.

Assumption of Co-Equal Efficiency

        Another strong counterargument: the visual balance of the graph reflects the note’s naive assumption of strategic parity. What if the true length under the curve of one of the pillars is ten times larger than the other two combined? None of this is meaningful if one has reason to believe that, for example, the orange curve (inner alignment) is a tidal wave while the other two are ripples.

        This is a great point, and it is one worth convincing other people on. If one kind of doom is way more likely than the others, or way deadlier in a relative sense than the other forms of doom, we should not be wasting our time. I only currently hold this view because it is my form of a maximally agnostic prior.

        But if a tidal wave is approaching just beyond the horizon, and the only thing you know is that a tidal wave is coming, but not which direction it is coming from, and it is possible that there might be more than one, doesn’t it make sense to lay sandbags in all directions? And consider this: if the first point holds true, and one pillar ends up actually being 95% of all the danger we face because things are just that correlated. What if we succeed? Would there still not be a danger worth staying awake at night for? Given the infinite negative utility of x-risk, even small probabilities of distinct failure modes demand attention.

        Still, this is not a point that is worth defending simply for the sake of ‘saving face’. If I am wrong about this, it can only be a good thing. Having to worry about one thing is unquestionably better than having to worry about three. For the critics that hold this opinion: you should make every effort to win. Failure to recognize an asymmetry here might well make all the difference between a problem we solve, and one we give up on before even trying.

The Static Representation

        The idea that there are three meaningfully distinct pillars, that they might have some overlap, or that there might nonetheless still be some non-overlap, are all constructed assumptions from a static snapshot in time. Another good critique is that this does not capture the genre of dynamic, cascading failures, where a middle alignment failure at x=50 does not simply stay there, but actively creates sudden, new failures at x=40 and x=60. It might even be what precisely triggers the sudden collapse of technical efforts to solve outer alignment, causing the rapid expansion of the area under the blue curve, which then shortly engulfs or distorts everything else.

        I cannot really disagree with this really. The point that things can change, and that they do change, and that we don’t know what we don’t know, seems rationally watertight. All I can say is that if you thought I had the raw intelligence or technical skill to write code for dynamic graphs or evolving state space systems, you have severely overestimated me, and this is why I think you should probably be the one helping to work on this problem and not me: my optimism may be a function of stupidity, not insight.

item.title: Concrete Generalist Projects in AI Safety (and how to do them)
item.description:
The AI safety ecosystem is still in need of generalists: people who will go out and solve the tasks that people who feel limited by their job description won’t address. This post will explain how to break into generalist work, then provide an important set of projects that, if completed, could strengthen many crucial parts of the AI safety ecosystem, as well as your own career. 

TL;DR

If you’re looking for something concrete to do, there are a bunch of good entry points:

  • Find a project: browse SPAR’s Generalist Projects, join the Generalist Megastream, look through projects on Mangrove, or browse this fieldbuilding/project spreadsheet and Atlas Computing’s Resilience Gap Map.
  • Get support: apply to Genstream (deadline August 14), indicate interest in the Generator Residency, or check out MATS’s Founding & Fieldbuilding track and Catalyst.
  • Get funding: BlueDot Rapid Grants fund projects up to $10k; there are also quick funding opportunities and career-transition grants from Coefficient Giving and BlueDot.
  • If you’re a student: join or start a university AI safety group; Pathfinder and the AI Safety Seeding Initiative can help with mentorship and funding.

The rest of the post has more detail on choosing projects, getting mentorship, and other ways to get involved.

If you’re a…

University Student: get heavily involved with your university AI safety group. University groups are real, impactful organizations, and they can be run as such. 

If your school doesn’t have a group, you should start one. Convincing an equally talented person to join AI safety can straightforwardly double your impact, and many of the most impactful people working in the field today credit their university groups for convincing them to make this career choice. 

A university group is also a great place to cut your teeth doing generalist work. Most group organizers find themselves working on operations, strategy, events, headhunting, and research in a single week, testing their fit for each type of work and operating under enviably tight feedback loops. It’s rare that an early-college generalist finds a better opportunity for both impact and career capital than “making their school’s group a lot better,” which is why many of the field’s best generalists were once university group organizers. 

If you would like to get access to funding or mentorship, the Pathfinder Fellowship and the AI Safety Seeding Initiative are both fantastic resources to get mentorship and funding. University groups can run existing educational programs like ARENA, or they can support students’ efforts to get into SPAR, MATS, Generator, or one of the many other advanced fellowships that teach people how to do impactful work.

Early or Mid-Career Professional: Make sure you have relevant context on the AI safety space. Take some BlueDot courses, meet people at AI safety events, and read voraciously from a variety of sources. 

Once you have a general understanding of the field, look into projects. Completing an AI safety project is a good way to support the field, meet new people, and gain valuable skills and context. You can just do many of these things; you don’t need permission or a full-time role to contribute!

This section is basically a TL;DR version of 80k Hours’ posts on how to get into AI safety in 3 months. There’s a wealth of information on their Substack, their website, and they just released a book!

Projects that should get done

The AI safety space is littered with unresolved problems and inefficiencies, because many of the people who were skilled enough to notice these problems don’t have enough spare time to address them. While preparing for the Generator Residency, we conducted interviews with dozens of AI safety professionals from organizations like Coefficient Giving, AI Futures Project, Forethought, and more.

The residents couldn’t do all of them, but that doesn't mean they shouldn’t be done. 

Some of these projects might make the talent pipeline more efficient, making it easier for passionate people to learn about AI safety and gain the skills that make them impactful. Other projects might improve our data collection systems, make concerns about existential risks visible to a broader audience, make it easier to convert political will into impactful legislation, or fill some broader need that can’t be easily described. 

This list is far from exhaustive, and many of the programs listed will be continuously maintained with new projects as the needs of the field evolve. We hope that this section serves as a jumping-off point for you to explore the programs and shared resources outlined below.

SPAR Generalist Projects

SPAR’s generalist projects are a new category under SPAR with mentors from Generator, Constellation, Kairos, universities, and other AI safety organizations on projects in fieldbuilding, communications, research, and organizational infrastructure.

Current projects include:

  • Revitalizing AI Lab Watch
  • Curated AI Safety Comment Threads
  • Launching an AI Safety Comms Fellowship for Undergrads
  • Update the AI Safety Fieldmap
  • Resources and Playbooks for University Groups

Plus a dozen more, as well as a Generalist Megastream for strong applicants who do not see a perfect fit among the existing listings. Applications close August 18.

Mangrove

We’ve added a number of projects we find promising to Mangrove, a platform for coordinating AI safety projects and communities. 

We think a lot about AI safety talent pipelines, and by far the biggest drop-off for potential generalists is the stage between “having context in AI safety” and “building signal to get into fellowships”. Much time gets lost due to lack of coordination, and much motivation gets lost due to lack of accountability and community. 

We’re excited about Mangrove as a place for people to hit the ground running on interesting projects, while developing credibility and connections in the space. Mangrove is in development, and plans to host hackathons, community projects for university groups, a contracting platform for orgs (!), and more. 

Mangrove’s official launch announcement is coming in a few days, but you can check out the platform right now.

Some projects we seeded on Mangrove:

  • Turn AI Safety Findings into Shareable Visuals
  • The Public Cares About AI - Just Not the Right Parts
  • Evaluating AI-Generated Research Forums
  • Build Pastcasting Workshops on US Government Crisis Response

Non-project shaped projects

A lot of generalist shaped things don’t have discrete projects, and rather require building specific skills like effective comms, hiring/recruiting, org strategy, management, and much more, to pick up dropped balls. As a sample of these sorts of fuzzier projects:

Consider being an influencer: As “warning shots” become scarier and more frequent, there’s potential and demand for high-quality media that connect these events to broader AI safety concerns and convert public will into action. Some great media has come out of the AI safety ecosystem as the Overton window is shifting, and programs like The Frame and Tarbell have emerged to target this. 

Political organizing: There’s a lot of useful work in recruiting people, running events, building local groups, organizing constituent outreach, and helping turn public will into useful legislation and strong leadership. This work is often bottlenecked on reliable organizers, and many consider it incredibly high-leverage. Political organizing can become quite sensitive and prone to backfire risk, so if you’re interested in this, we recommend filling out this short form before launching something yourself and we'll connect you with someone who can advise you.

Writing: Writing publicly is one of the fastest ways to build a track record. The spreadsheet below includes a running list of posts people want written. 

Other Project Lists

  • This spreadsheet has an active list of fieldbuilding projects, university outreach ideas, and blog posts that could be valuable to write. It also has descriptions of various problems, solution directions, theories of change, and people associated with these projects.
  • Atlas Computing’s Resilience Gap Map provides a list of AI-related projects that need to be addressed, as well as the critical assumptions behind working on them.
  • This is a list of lists of project ideas in AI Safety. It has many lists, including research project lists and fieldbuilding lists.
  • Some schemes for AI safety by Austin Chen. Manifund and Mox are running fellowships like Surplus to support these. 

Getting Support 

Programs

As a general rule, you should be applying for more things. New programs are springing up to accelerate generalists: 

  • Consider indicating interest in the Generator Residency, a 3-6 month long program dedicated to rapidly upskilling generalists.
  • MATS also has a Founding and Fieldbuilding path.
  • Catalyst is a 10-week remote program for undergraduates to work on impactful projects.
  • [Applications close August 14th] Genstream is a one-week, in-person AI safety program in London for aspiring generalists.

Funding 

Many people are too scared to apply for funding, when probably they shouldn't be! Even if you don’t get the money, oftentimes submitting a (non-slop) grant proposal can be a good forcing function for execution. 

  • BlueDot Rapid Grants give out grants of up to $10k, with an average turnaround time of 3 days. They are happy to fund: Compute and API credits, events and meetups, research access, travel, community chapters, project tooling. Wildcards welcome.
  • Austin Chen’s list of quick funding opportunities
  • Coefficient Giving’s career development and transition funding is targeted for more mid to senior career people, giving runway for up to 6 months to explore AI safety careers. BlueDot also gives out career transition grants. 

Advice on getting mentorship

It can be extremely helpful to know people in the community who can give you mentorship. A good mentor can make a big difference in acquiring taste, skills, and connections. Many of the best projects require specific context to complete well. 

As a general rule, your bar for reaching out to people is too high. 

For example, if you’re especially interested in a series of blog posts someone has written, consider reaching out to discuss the content of their post further (but try not to ask questions that you can easily answer by reading more of their work, or a 2 minute search). 

Alternatively, if there are sets of projects you are interested in pursuing, consider reaching out to people who have done similar work, or find a SPAR mentor who can help you do so. You can reach the authors of this post at roman.alex.ross@gmail.com, viceversa1024@gmail.com (Harry), or helenatran9305@gmail.com, and you can meet many more people at events like EA Global or a Global Challenges Project workshop.

A final note

AI safety can be a confusing field to enter, and a lot of useful context lives inside organizations, private conversations, and people’s heads. Still, we think one of the fastest ways to build that context is to work on something concrete. Projects expose you to fast feedback from the outside world, give you reasons to talk to knowledgeable people, and get you oriented faster than reading alone.
